content.text: Lesson 1 Overview

In this lesson, we will explore five key renewable energy technologies that are playing a pivotal role in climate mitigation and shaping the global energy transition. While there are numerous emerging and nascent technologies on the horizon, the focus here will be on those that are already having a significant impact or show strong potential to drive the transition to a low-carbon future. Understanding these technologies is crucial for advancing sustainable energy solutions and achieving the goals of reducing greenhouse gas emissions and limiting global warming.

content.title: Key Concepts
content.intro: Explore foundational ideas from this lesson.

concepts.title: climate risk in the power sector
concepts.body: Climate risk in the power sector refers to the potential negative impacts of climate change on energy production, distribution, and infrastructure, including extreme weather events, changing temperature patterns, and regulatory changes that can affect the reliability and sustainability of power supply.

concepts.title: climate vulnerability
concepts.body: Climate vulnerability refers to the degree to which a system, community, or individual is susceptible to the adverse effects of climate change, including extreme weather events, rising sea levels, and changing climate patterns.

concepts.title: energy reliability
concepts.body: Energy reliability refers to the ability of an energy system to consistently provide power without interruptions or failures, ensuring that electricity is available when needed.

content.text: CLIMATE CHANGE MITIGATION

Climate change mitigation refers to any action taken by governments, businesses or people to reduce or prevent greenhouse gases, or to enhance carbon sinks that remove them from the atmosphere. Mitigation efforts include transitioning to renewable energy sources, enhancing energy efficiency, adopting regenerative agricultural practices and protecting and restoring forests and critical ecosystems. Effective mitigation requires a whole-of-society approach 💬️ and structural transformations to reduce emissions and limit global warming to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels.

By the end of 2024, global renewable energy capacity had reached approximately 4,448 GW. Solar power remained the dominant source, contributing 1,865 GW to the total.

Hydropower and wind energy also played significant roles, with installed capacities of 1,283 GW and 1,133 GW, respectively. Other renewable sources included 151 GW from bioenergy, 15 GW from geothermal energy, and 0.5 GW from marine energy.

Following these updated figures, we will take a closer look at five key renewable technologies, examining their advancements, applications, and role in the global energy transition.

Solar power is one of the cleanest and most abundant renewable energy sources available. It can be harnessed through various technologies, such as solar photovoltaics (PV), concentrated solar power 💬️ (CSP), and solar thermal systems. Solar PV technology is the most widespread, transforming sunlight into electricity via silicon semiconductors. However, PV systems require battery storage to retain electricity for nighttime use. In 2023, solar PV accounted for 346.9 GW of the 473 GW added globally, about 73% of new renewable capacity. CSP, on the other hand, uses mirrors to concentrate sunlight, generating heat for power production, and it can store energy for use at night. In 2020, CSP’s installed capacity reached 7 gigawatts, showing significant growth since 2010.

Solar power plays a critical role in reducing greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. For example, solar PV produces about 43-45 grams of CO2 per kWh through its lifecycle as discussed in the previous chapter. When replacing fossil fuel power with solar PV, an acre of solar panels can save up to 198 metric tons of CO2 annually. Additionally, the cost of solar panels has dramatically dropped, with prices falling 93% from 2010 to 2020, making solar power the most affordable energy source in many regions.

The solar energy market has driven job creation as well. In 2023, approximately 7.1 million people were employed in solar PV, with China, dominating the workforce with 4.6 million jobs. Employment in clean energy continued to surpass fossil fuel jobs, reaching 34.8 million positions compared to 32.6 million in the fossil fuel sector.
Challenges to Solar Power Implementation
While solar power has immense potential, there are challenges to widespread implementation:

content.title: Grid Integration
content.body: Solar energy is variable and dependent on weather and location. Managing this variability requires investments in grid infrastructure, storage, and demand response.

content.title: Cost in Low-Income Countries
content.body: Solar projects face higher capital costs in developing countries due to factors such as governance issues and currency fluctuations.

content.title: Access to Funding
content.body: Solar transitions in low-income countries are often hindered by limited access to finance. Wealthier countries, though more capable of investing, still face issues with equitable distribution of technologies and grid integration

content.text:
Wind power harnesses the kinetic energy of the wind through turbines that convert it into electrical energy, producing minimal greenhouse gas emissions compared to other energy sources. Over the past decade, wind technology has seen significant innovations, improving efficiency, power, and capacity while reducing noise. Wind installations now include onshore, offshore, and floating platforms capable of withstanding extreme conditions, such as hurricane-force winds. Offshore wind, with its stronger and more consistent winds, is expected to grow as siting challenges are addressed. Wind power currently accounts for 6-7% of global electricity, with substantial potential to meet global energy needs.
Wind energy is a crucial component of global climate strategies, particularly under the IEA Net Zero Emissions (NZE) Scenario, as emphasized in the UAE Consensus, which calls for doubling energy efficiency 💬️ and tripling renewable energy capacity by 2030. In 2022, wind power grew by 17%, contributing to a combined 12% share of global electricity generation alongside solar PV. Wind energy's near-zero greenhouse gas emissions and high energy return on energy invested (EROEI) make it an essential solution for reducing emissions.
Additionally, wind power supports job creation, particularly in China and Europe, with 1.4 million jobs in 2022. Wind turbines have an operational lifespan of 20 years, running nearly emissions-free after offsetting construction emissions within 3-6 months.
Challenges to Wind Power Implementation

content.title: Volatile Markets
content.body: Supply chain issues, rising demand, and cost increases (raw materials, shipping, interest rates, and inflation) have delayed or shelved some wind projects. This is also in several cases accompanied by weak political will.

content.title: Cost for Lower-Income Countries
content.body: Access to capital and higher project financing costs in developing countries pose challenges for wind energy deployment, particularly for onshore wind projects.

content.title: High Initial Costs
content.body: Setting up a wind farm involves significant upfront investment in turbines and associated infrastructure.

content.title: Grid Integration
content.body: Integrating variable wind power into the existing electricity grid requires sophisticated management systems to maintain grid stability.

content.text:
Kazakhstan had long been renowned for its richness not only in oil, coal, or gas but also for something intangible: wind. However, its energy system was at a crossroads despite being rich in fossil fuels. One of the main reasons behind the greenhouse gas emissions in Kazakhstan was the combustion of fossil fuels, and its energy sector alone accounted for up to 87% of its total emissions (Almaz, Yohji, & Keiichi, 2011, pp. 1-2). Multiple villages and cities were affected by the pollutants emitted from the aging energy plants, leading to environmental degradation and public health risks. Kazakhstan’s solution was found in the untapped resource of wind. Thus, the Wind Power Market Development project launched through the collaboration of the GEF, the Government of Kazakhstan, and the UNDP aimed to establish a sustainable wind energy 💬️ sector in Kazakhstan.
The country’s wind potential, estimated at a staggering 929 billion kWh annually, was to be utilized through the project to reduce greenhouse gas emissions (Lettice, 2014, Executive Summary). Despite this potential, critical barriers stalled progress, including financial, institutional, information, awareness, and capacity barriers (Mid-Term Evaluation, 2007, Executive Summary). The significant barriers identified during the preparatory phase of the project included securing foreign and domestic investments, underdeveloped technical capacity, minimal awareness of wind energy’s potential, financial barriers, and the absence of operational wind farms to offer a proof of concept. Moreover, the absence of dedicated regulatory frameworks and policies also posed significant challenges (Lettice, 2014, p. 34).

The project aimed to bring international expertise to the country and engage stakeholders, thereby contributing to the accelerated development of the local market. On the fiscal front, the project sought creative solutions to mitigate significant costs and risks associated with the early-stage investment (Final-term Evaluation, 2011, pp. 22-24). Despite being unable to realize the initially proposed 5 MW wind farm pilot project related to power purchase agreements and being unable to proceed, the project shifted course wisely. The project also facilitated the creation of the National Wind Power Development Program, which set ambitious targets for wind energy generation, aiming for 750 million kWh by 2015 and 5 billion kWh by 2030 (Lettice, 2014, pp. 21, 44).
The central takeaways of the project could be listed as follows:
The wind energy potential lacked commercial potential without a predictable and stable regulatory and legal landscape. The project refocused on setting the stage for wider market expansion rather than focusing on a single pilot project farm (Final-term Evaluation, 2011, Executive Summary).
The lack of a government-supported long-term power purchase support scheme was another significant hurdle. The Wind projects fail to capture interest in the absence of such a mechanism (Lettice, 2014, p. 47). This challenge is not limited to Kazakhstan; nations seeking to adopt a similar strategy must establish stable regulatory frameworks that encourage investments and lower financial risks (Final-term Evaluation, 2011, p. 14).

Bringing a vision to fruition in Kazakhstan, where the wind energy market was barely emerging, was a considerable undertaking. Nonetheless, the Wind Power Market Development Initiative took on the challenge with determination and thoughtful care, starting with a profound understanding of the local context. The key initial move was to build a robust regulatory and legal base. Working in close coordination with government partners, the project helped to support and develop the RES Law (Renewable Energy Resources), accompanied by clear rules that defined how to monitor the projects, link to the grid, and purchase renewable (sources) electricity. Inspiring local and international investors to believe in Wind Power in Kazakhstan, this legal framework became the foundation for future wind energy projects.

Available information, or the notable lack thereof, was yet another significant barrier. Developers were left in the dark, lacking proper data on wind potential and unable to initiate a wind project. Producing an online wind Atlas and meteorological monitoring at various sites helped close this gap. This new information enabled developers to pinpoint optimal investment locations grounded in solid scientific research. Moreover, dedicated initiatives focused on imparting practical expertise to professionals, such as the application of simulation tools such as WindPro and wind resource assessment, have been established.

At its core, the initiative was further beyond setting up wind turbines. Instead, it centered around developing an entire ecosystem required for the wind energy market to flourish. The main objective of the project was to promote the development of the wind power market in Kazakhstan by assisting the government in formulating a national program for wind energy development and local capacity building to develop wind energy projects in Kazakhstan. Furthermore, it aimed to monitor, analyze, and disseminate the lessons learned and experiences gained during the project’s implementation. To begin with, the primary focus of the initiative was to validate the feasibility of large-scale wind power in Kazakhstan through a pilot project aimed at generating 5 MW of wind energy (Terms of Reference for the Mid-term Evaluation of the UNDP/GEF Project, Introduction). However, it contributed only to one element of the solution. The real intervention stemmed from institutional capacity building and policy reforms.

The project collaborated with the government to develop an enabling legal and regulatory framework. Due to the project’s efforts, the government implemented a series of measures, including clear rules for power purchase agreements, feed-in tariffs, and optimized procedures for grid connection. These mechanisms helped in attracting sustained investment in the sector. Moreover, the project extended beyond collaborating with financiers and policymakers. Recognizing the need for skilled professionals in a sustainable market, it trained over 200 professionals and organized study tours and conferences, ensuring that Kazakhstan would have a ready pool of trained professionals capable of advancing the wind energy sector (Lettice, 2014, pp. 33-43).

The attempt to launch the pilot project was instrumental in revealing the logistical and institutional challenges, even though it did not come to realization. A major unanticipated issue that highlighted the value of integrated planning for all major transport modes was the difficulty transporting sizable turbine machinery to remote sites. It is evident from these lessons that adaptation is essential to accommodate the unique regulatory, infrastructure, and market dynamics of each setting for successful replication in other countries rather than simply mirroring the technical assessments of Kazakhstan (Lettice, 2014, p. 46) (Final-term Evaluation, 2011).

Although the incompletion of the pilot project could be perceived as a shortcoming, reallocating the project’s budget to strengthen institutional and policy frameworks, as well as capacity-building initiatives, likely delivered long-term benefits (Lettice, 2014). Ultimately, the larger lesson is that the development of a thriving renewable energy market relies on strategic foresight, adaptive policy frameworks, and consistent efforts to mitigate commercial risks.

content.title: C: Hydropower

content.text:
Hydropower is a significant renewable energy source that harnesses the potential energy of water flowing from higher to lower elevations. It can be categorized into different types, including storage dams and “run-of-river” systems. Large storage dams provide backup power and rapid response during outages, while run-of-river plants offer continuous base load energy. Hydropower is highly valuable for grid stability, providing fast-response generation and supporting frequency stability. However, its potential is influenced by climate-related changes in rainfall and ecosystems, with droughts posing a challenge.

Hydropower offers substantial carbon emissions reductions, saving up to 4 billion tonnes of CO2 annually compared to coal. It accounts for about 9% of global CO2 emissions reduction. In the IEA Net Zero Emissions by 2050 scenario, hydropower continues to grow at an average rate of 4% annually. There remains considerable untapped potential for hydropower development. Global technical potential is estimated at 14,576 TWh/year, over four times current generation levels. Africa, in particular, holds vast undeveloped potential, offering significant opportunities for growth.
Challenges to Hydro Power Implementation

content.title: High Initial Investment
content.body: Both large-scale hydropower projects and hydro mini-grids require significant upfront capital. This is often a barrier in developing countries with limited financial resources.

content.title: Infrastructure Limitations
content.body: Developing countries often lack the necessary infrastructure to support large-scale hydropower projects. This includes not only the physical infrastructure for dams but also transmission lines to distribute electricity.

content.title: Ecological and Social Impact
content.body: Hydropower projects can disrupt ecosystems, alter water flow, and negatively affect biodiversity. Large dams may also lead to community displacement, triggering social unrest.

content.title: Geopolitical Tensions
content.body: Hydropower development can exacerbate transboundary water disputes, especially in regions where multiple countries rely on shared water resources.

content.text:
geothermal energy 💬️ provides reliable, base-load power and heating/cooling from a widely available resource. It offers sustainable production and generates cost-effective, dispatchable power, unaffected by climate conditions. Geothermal energy has lower greenhouse gas emissions compared to traditional base-load thermal generation. In off-peak periods, it can also help recharge battery-powered vehicles, further reducing CO2 emissions.

Geothermal energy can become a key part of future electricity and heating systems, offering a clean and reliable energy source. Right now, geothermal meets less than 1% of global energy demand, and its use is mostly in countries with easily accessible, high-quality resources like the United States, Iceland, Indonesia, Türkiye, Kenya, and Italy.

Geothermal energy has the potential to significantly contribute to global electricity demand by 2050. Advancements in technology and reductions in project costs could enable the deployment of up to 800 gigawatts (GW) of geothermal capacity worldwide, generating nearly 6,000 terawatt-hours annually—equivalent to the current combined electricity consumption of the United States and India.

A notable advantage of geothermal power is its ability to provide continuous, baseload electricity. Geothermal plants can operate at full capacity 24/7, offering a reliable energy source. In 2023, global geothermal capacity had a utilization rate exceeding 75%, significantly higher than wind power's less than 30% and solar photovoltaic's (PV) less than 15%. Additionally, geothermal plants can operate flexibly, aiding in grid stabilization and complementing intermittent renewable sources like solar PV and wind.

The International Energy Agency (IEA) projects that, with appropriate support, costs for next-generation geothermal technologies could decrease by 80% by 2035. At this cost level, geothermal plants could produce electricity at approximately $50 per megawatt-hour (MWh), positioning them among the most affordable dispatchable low-emission electricity sources, comparable to or cheaper than hydro, nuclear, and bioenergy. Furthermore, geothermal energy would be highly competitive with solar and wind power when paired with battery storage 💬️.
Challenges to Geothermal Energy Implementation

content.title: Global Coordination and Classifications
content.body: The lack of standardized guidelines for geothermal resource assessment, efficiency, and environmental impact hampers transparency and comparability. This hinders progress and accurate assessments of how geothermal energy is operating and performing. This leads to ambiguity in reporting and a limited understanding of what needs to be done differently.

content.title: Cost and technology
content.body: High-grade geothermal resources have restricted geographic distribution. There are cost and technological hurdles to using low-grade geothermal resources and EGS. The levelized cost of geothermal energy has increased 36% from 2010-2021, more than any other energy source examined in that research. High-quality geothermal resources are already economically competitive with market energy costs in many areas. Public and private research funding and favorable deployment rules may be required to develop and commercialize lower-grade hydrothermal deposits. The effectiveness of these efforts may play an important role in determining the magnitude of geothermal energy's contributions to long-term GHG emissions reductions.

content.text:
Hydrogen is a versatile energy carrier, with clean hydrogen produced from renewables helping sectors like long-haul transport, chemicals, and iron and steel. Blue hydrogen, made from natural gas through methods like steam methane reforming and autothermal reforming, produces CO2 but can capture and store it. Green hydrogen, produced through electrolysis 💬️ using renewable electricity, has no harmful by-products.

Hydrogen plays a fundamental role in mitigating sectors that have proven hard to abate. Global hydrogen demand grew by 3% in 2022 to 95 million tonnes. There are mainly heavy industry, shipping, long-distance land transport, and aviation. Implementing clean hydrogen provides relatively low technical challenges in the refining and fertilizer sectors, as it can be a like-for-like substitution for others. More than 393 agreements were made related to hydrogen in 2022.

While this marks significant progress for a growing sector, most production is still in the planning or early stages. To fully realize the project pipeline, the sector must grow at an extraordinary rate of over 90% annually from 2024 to 2030, far surpassing the growth of solar PV during its peak expansion.
Government Policies and Regulatory Frameworks

content.title: Incentives and Subsidies
content.body: Governments can enhance the attractiveness of renewable investments by offering financial incentives such as subsidies, tax breaks, and feed-in tariffs that guarantee fixed prices for renewable energy.

content.title: Clear Regulatory Frameworks
content.body: Establishing transparent and supportive regulations can simplify the approval processes for renewable projects, reducing bureaucratic delays and building investor confidence.

content.text: Challenges to Geothermal Energy Implementation

content.title: High Costs
content.body: Hydrogen production is expensive, often 2-3 times more costly than fossil fuel alternatives. Pipelines, fuel cells, and storage tanks also carry high costs.

content.title: Lack of Standards
content.body: The absence of globally accepted standards for measuring and certifying the greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions of hydrogen production creates inconsistencies across markets, complicating efforts to compare its environmental impact. Traditional classifications based on color labels (e.g., green, blue, gray hydrogen) lack precision and fail to account for varying emissions intensities.

content.title: Cross-Border Cooperation
content.body: Transporting and storing hydrogen requires significant infrastructure investment and international collaboration, as imported hydrogen is often cheaper than local production.

content.text: innovative financing 💬️ Mechanisms

content.title: Blended Finance and De-risking Mechanisms
content.body: Mobilizing private capital is essential to bridge the energy finance gap. Expanding financial structures such as blended finance, alongside financial de-risking mechanisms like guarantee schemes will for sure encourage private sector participation.

content.title: International Financial Support
content.body: Actively seeking partnerships with international financial institutions to access grants and concessional loans aimed at renewable energy projects is important.

content.title: Water Consumption
content.body: The production of hydrogen, particularly through electrolysis, requires significant water resources. In areas where water scarcity is an issue, this could pose a serious environmental concern.

content.title: Safety Concerns
content.body: Hydrogen storage and transport require high-pressure systems, raising concerns about potential leaks, explosions, and safety risks to nearby communities.

content.title: Unequal distribution of benefits
content.body: Like with any technology, concerns exist about ensuring equitable access to hydrogen technology and its benefits across different socioeconomic groups and regions.

content.text: Infrastructure Development

content.title: Grid Modernization
content.body: Upgrading existing grid infrastructure is essential for accommodating the variable nature of renewables. Investments in smart grid technologies can improve reliability and efficiency in energy distribution.

content.title: Energy Storage Solutions
content.body: Implementing energy storage systems is crucial for managing the intermittency of renewable sources, allowing excess energy to be stored for use during low generation periods.

takeaways.title: Diverse Renewable Technologies are Key to Emission Reductions.
takeaways.description: Solar, wind, hydropower, geothermal, and hydrogen are playing a crucial role in reducing greenhouse gas emissions and accelerating the global energy transition. Each technology has unique advantages, such as solar PV’s affordability, wind energy’s scalability, hydropower’s grid stability, geothermal’s reliability, and hydrogen’s potential for hard-to-abate sectors.

takeaways.title: Implementation Challenges Must Be Addressed.
takeaways.description: While renewable energy technologies offer significant benefits, their implementation faces challenges, including high initial investment costs, grid integration issues, financing constraints, and infrastructure limitations, particularly in developing countries.

takeaways.title: Strategic Approaches are Essential for Scaling Renewable Energy.
takeaways.description: Policy incentives, innovative financing (e.g., blended finance and concessional loans), infrastructure development (grid modernization and energy storage), capacity building, and community engagement are key strategies for scaling up renewable energy deployment, ensuring equitable access, and supporting a just energy transition.
